sections.title_en: 1. The Redemption from Egypt and the Redemption of Slaves and Workers
sections.body_en:
The redemption from Egypt was not only a private redemption, in which one of the nations merited to be freed from its cruel enslavers. In the Exodus from Egypt the worth of the people of Israel was revealed, and the worth of the divine morality that Israel bequeaths to the world.

In the Exodus from Egypt the value of freedom was revealed, which is one of the foundations of morality. For all the nations of the world, when they succeed in overcoming their enslavers, become proud and make themselves enslavers of their former masters. Whereas Israel, even after the Egyptians had been utterly struck, did not try to overcome them and enslave them, but only to go out to freedom, as Hashem commanded Moshe.

And likewise we were commanded that even when we have slaves – for such is the way of the world: there are rich and there are poor, and when the ability to earn a living is very constrained there are also slaves – nevertheless we were commanded not to work the slaves with crushing labour, as it is said (Vayikra 25:43): "You shall not rule over him with rigour, but you shall fear your God." And the point is that a person should impose on his slave only work that he needs to have done, but he should not impose on him tasks for which he has no need and whose only purpose is to afflict or humiliate him. For example, one who sees his slave idle should not say to him: please heat this water for me, or: cool it for me, when he has no wish to drink it. And likewise he should not say to him: hoe in such-and-such a place, when his whole aim is to keep him busy and work him without having any benefit from it (Sifra ibid.). And likewise one should not say to him: hoe in such-and-such a place until I come, for when he gives him work without limit, he afflicts his soul; rather, he should say to him: work here until such-and-such an hour (and see Rambam, Laws of Slaves 1:6-7, 9, 8).

Admittedly, this mitzva applies to a slave; but the Sefer Ha-Ḥinukh (mitzva 346) wrote that towards poor workers too it is fitting for a person to be very careful in this.

And similarly it is written in Sha'arei Teshuva of Rabbeinu Yona (Gate 3, 60): "A person should not make his fellows serve him; and if his fear is upon them, or they are ashamed to refuse his word, he should not command them to do anything small or great, except for their own wish and benefit – even to heat a jug of water or to go out on his errand to the city street to buy as much as a loaf of bread. But a person who does not behave properly may be commanded to do whatever one wishes," because by making him work he corrects his bad character and keeps him from the idleness that leads to sin.

sections.title_en: 2. They Shall Not Be Sold as Slaves Are Sold, and the Freedom of the Worker
sections.body_en:
We were commanded not to sell Jewish slaves in the manner in which a slave is sold, as it is said (Vayikra 25:42): "For they are My servants, whom I brought out of the land of Egypt; they shall not be sold as slaves are sold."

First, there is in this mitzva an instruction that when a Jew is forced to sell himself as a Hebrew slave, we should not sell him by public announcement: here is a slave, whoever wishes to buy him, let him come. Rather, he should be sold discreetly.

And the Sages learned a further law from this mitzva: a worker who hired himself out to work for his fellow is permitted to retract in the middle of his work and say, I do not want to continue working. For example, if a person hired his fellow to hoe in his field all that day, the worker is permitted to stop his work in the middle of the day even though he undertook to work a whole day. And even if they have already paid him his whole wage, he can say, I do not want to continue working, and return to them their money for the remainder of the work. And the reason for this is that this is his basic right as a free person, to retract from his undertaking to work, as it is said (Vayikra 25:55): "For to Me the children of Israel are servants; they are My servants," and the Sages expounded (Bava Metzia 10a): "and not servants to servants" – that they should work against their will because they undertook to work. Admittedly, it is clear that this is not a proper thing to do, that a person should go back on his word, and he is "lacking in trustworthiness" (see above 2:9), and the employer may hold a grievance against him; but the employer cannot oblige him to continue working.

But if, because he stops his work in the middle of the time, the employer will suffer a financial loss, the worker is forbidden to stop his work, because a person is forbidden to cause damage to his fellow. And he must continue the work until the employer can find a replacement for him, in a way that no damage will be caused to him (SA ḤM 333:3-5).

sections.title_en: 3. The Treatment of Slaves and Setting Them Free
sections.body_en:
Before Hashem brought Israel out of Egypt, He told Moshe to command them about 'setting slaves free', and this is what is said (Shemot 6:13): "And the Lord spoke to Moshe and to Aharon, and commanded them concerning the children of Israel." That is, after they go out to freedom and enter the Land, and, as is the way of the world, there will presumably be rich and poor, and at times it will happen to a man that he loses all he has until he cannot sustain himself and is forced to sell himself as a slave – be very careful to keep the mitzvot of the Torah and to free him at his time (based on Yerushalmi Rosh Ha-Shana 3:5).

If the court sold him because he stole and cannot pay his debt, he is freed at the end of six years, from day to day; and if the Jubilee falls in the middle of the six years, he is freed at the Jubilee. And when he sells himself because of his economic situation, he can sell himself for more years, and at the end of those years one is obligated to free him. And likewise one is obligated to free him when the Jubilee arrives, even if the Jubilee arrives within the years for which he agreed to sell himself (Rambam, Laws of Slaves 2:2-3).

And when he is freed, it is a mitzva to give him gifts from things that produce fruit, such as the yield of grain, grapes and sheep. And the main thing is that the value of the grant amount to at least thirty sela (Rambam ibid. 3:14), a sum from which one person can live for about five years! (based on Rabbi Benish, author of the book Middot Ve-shi'urei Torah).

At the end of the days of the First Temple the officers and the rich sinned and did not free their slaves as the Torah commands. The moral right to live as a free people was annulled. The destiny for which Israel had gone out of Egypt was violated. And the Babylonians began to besiege Jerusalem with a great army. And behold, the officers and the rich were roused to repentance, and freed their slaves as the Torah commands. And a miracle happened to them: the siege was lifted, and the Babylonians were forced to leave Jerusalem and go out towards Egypt to war. And when the officers saw that there was relief, they went back to enslaving the slaves. "And the word of the Lord came to Yirmiyahu from the Lord, saying: Thus says the Lord, the God of Israel: I made a covenant with your fathers on the day that I brought them out of the land of Egypt, out of the house of bondage, saying: At the end of seven years you shall let go every man his brother who is a Hebrew… But you turned and profaned My name, and caused every man his servant and every man his handmaid, whom you had let go free at their pleasure, to return; and you brought them into subjection, to be to you for servants and for handmaids…" Therefore the Lord proclaimed liberty for all the calamities that would come upon Israel (Yirmiyahu 34).

Such is the life of the chosen people in the world: everything depends on the moral state. When they descend, they descend to the dust of the earth; and when they ascend, they ascend to the stars in the heavens.

The Torah established that a person who injures his fellow is punished measure for measure: "an eye for an eye, a tooth for a tooth, a hand for a hand, a foot for a foot, a burn for a burn, a wound for a wound, a bruise for a bruise" (Shemot 21:24-25). But the Sages explained that the meaning is that the one who injured pays money according to the value of the eye or the tooth or the hand or the foot (Bava Kamma 84a). And the question is: how can the Sages expound the verse and explain it otherwise than its plain meaning?

Our teacher and master Rabbi Tzvi Yehuda Ha-Kohen Kook ztz"l explained this topic fundamentally. The Torah is made up of two parts, the Written Torah and the Oral Torah. There is no other possibility of revealing the divine matter, because the divine matter is higher and loftier than the definitions graspable by our intellect; therefore the one divine matter is revealed to us in these two faces of the Written Torah and the Oral Torah, and together the completeness of the Torah is revealed.

Like a family in which there are a father and a mother, so in the Torah there are these two aspects, with the Written Torah filling the role of the father and the Oral Torah the role of the mother (based on Berakhot 35a).

"Of course, between the father and the mother there is no dispute but domestic peace, for it is all one complete matter. And behold, the son caused anger, and his father takes a strap in his hand to whip him – immediately the mother, who manages the household, leaps up, grabs the father's hand and stops him: 'Wait! It is true that he sinned, but I will arrange the educational matters of the house.' It was enough at that moment that the father held the strap in his hand; his intention was only to threaten…"

So the Written Torah expresses itself with full force against one who raises his hand against his fellow and injures him – "an eye for an eye"; but how in practice the repair is arranged, the Oral Torah explains: that it is by money. Thus in the end there will be a more fitting punishment, and proper compensation for the injured party (based on Siḥot Ha-Ratziyah, Shemot pp. 234-235; the source of the parable is the Zohar, Shemot 190b).[1]

notes_en.en: Even according to the plain meaning one must explain as the Sages did, as Rabbi Avraham Ibn Ezra wrote in his commentary on Shemot 21:24: "Rav Saadia said: we cannot explain this verse according to its literal meaning. For if a person struck his fellow's eye, and a third of the light of his eyes departed, how is it possible that the striker would be struck such a blow without addition or subtraction?" That is, it is not possible to cause damage exactly as the one who injured did, and therefore, in order to carry out the punishment, one must explain that the meaning is to assess it in money, and so the reckoning comes out 'an eye for an eye'.

sections.title_en: 5. The Mitzva of Burial and the Prohibition of Leaving the Dead Overnight
sections.body_en:
It is a mitzva to bury the dead, as it is said (Devarim 21:23): "You shall surely bury him on that day." And even a person who commanded his sons not to bury him is not listened to; rather, he is buried, because if they do not bury him there will be from this shame and disgrace to all living people, that the body of a person like them lies in disgrace (SA YD 348:3). That is, in the mitzva of burial there is honour for all the people who live; and therefore when the deceased has no family, all the people of the place are commanded to bury him.

And the mitzva is to bury the body in the earth, and there are two main reasons for this: a) to hide the shame of death, since it is a result of the sin of the first man; b) there is atonement in burial in the earth (see Sanhedrin 46b).

It is a mitzva to bury the dead promptly, and it is forbidden to leave his body overnight without burial. And whoever leaves his dead overnight transgresses a negative prohibition, as it is said (Devarim 21:23): "His body shall not remain all night upon the tree, but you shall surely bury him on that day." And in the view of many poskim, if the deceased died during the day, there is a positive mitzva to bury him before sunset, as it is said: "You shall surely bury him on that day" (Ha-Ḥinukh 537; MB 72:6). And the Ramban wrote that one who leaves his dead overnight in the Land of Israel transgresses a further prohibition, as it is said (Devarim 21:23): "And you shall not defile your land, which the Lord your God gives you for an inheritance."

And when they did not manage to bury him by sunset, or he died in the evening, the mitzva is to bury him by the end of the night; and if they did not bury him at night and dawn broke, they have transgressed the prohibition of "it shall not remain all night" (Radbaz). And those responsible for this are the relatives, who are commanded to bury their dead. And this is the honour of the dead, that he is buried as early as possible, for the essence of a person is the soul within him, and when the soul has left him there is great disgrace in delaying his body without burial. Further, since man was created in the image of God, when his form is disgraced, as it were the honour of Heaven too is impaired; and therefore we were commanded not to leave the dead overnight.

But for the sake of things necessary for the honour of the dead it is permitted to leave him overnight: if one needs to wait in order to bring him shrouds and a coffin, or in order to inform his relatives, it is permitted to leave him overnight. And likewise when he died in the evening, and several hours are needed to publicise the time of his funeral so that his acquaintances can accompany him, it is permitted to postpone the funeral to the next day (SA YD 357:1).

And some say that although they permitted leaving him overnight for the honour of the dead, this is on condition that no more than twenty-four hours pass from the moment of death until burial (Responsa Divrei Malkiel 2:95). And for a very great need it is customary to be lenient even beyond twenty-four hours, but one does not leave him for two days.

And in Jerusalem the custom is that even for the honour of the dead one does not leave the dead overnight. Within the walls of Jerusalem the custom is binding, and in the other neighbourhoods of the city it is customary to be stricter than in the rest of the country; but for a great need the dead is left overnight.

It is a great mitzva to eulogise the dead properly, as it is said (Bereshit 23:2): "And Avraham came to eulogise Sara and to weep for her." And the Sages said (Shabbat 105b): "Whoever weeps for a worthy person – all his sins are forgiven him." And it may perhaps be explained that one who weeps for a worthy person shows of himself that he knows what is good and what is bad, and this knowledge reaches the chambers of his soul; consequently it becomes clear that he does not agree with and accept his sins, and he is in the category of a true penitent.

And the point of the eulogy is to raise the voice and rouse the public to weeping, as the Sages said (Berakhot 6b): "The reward of a eulogy is in raising the voice," that is, the reward of the eulogy is the raising of the voice of weeping. And likewise Rav asked Rav Shmuel bar Shilat that after his death he exert himself in his eulogy so that the participants would be roused to weeping (Shabbat 153a). Being roused to weep for a worthy person who has died rouses the public to repentance, and it also helps to increase the merits of the deceased, that through his eulogy they were roused to repentance.

And if the deceased is a Torah scholar, one must be doubly careful in his eulogy. And the Sages said (ibid.): "Whoever is lax in the eulogy of a sage deserves to be buried alive, and does not live long." And the reason is that if he does not know how to value the Torah and the mitzvot, he does not know the value of life, and therefore it is not fitting that he live long.

And since it is hard to be precise in saying praises, it is better to add to the praises than to subtract (Arukh Ha-Shulḥan YD 344:6). But it is forbidden to exaggerate the praise of the deceased with things that are not in him. And whoever overstates the praise of the deceased causes evil to himself and to the dead (SA YD 344:1). And the reason the eulogist who overstates the praise of a deceased is punished is that when bad people are praised as the good are praised, the righteous become equal in people's eyes to the wicked, and truth is absent. And the dead too who was praised excessively is punished, for as a result they examine his judgement more closely in Heaven, and every praise that was said about him becomes for him a reminder of sin (Rosh).

And one who has no virtues, but suffered pains in his life or in his death – his sufferings are mentioned, and by this the public is roused to grieve and weep for him (see Mo'ed Katan 28b).

And for sages their wisdom is mentioned, and for the pious their piety is mentioned.

The trait of anger is a very bad trait. And the Sages said that one who is angry is like an idolater: "One who tears his garments in his anger, and one who breaks his vessels in his anger, and one who scatters his money in his anger – let him be in your eyes like an idolater; for such is the craft of the evil inclination: today it says to him, do this, and tomorrow it says to him, do that, until it says to him, worship idols, and he goes and worships." And Rabbi Avin said there that the source for this is from the verse (Tehillim 81:10): "There shall be no strange god in you, neither shall you worship any foreign god" – what is the strange god that is within a person's body? You must say, this is the evil inclination (Shabbat 105b). And they further said: "Whoever is angry – all kinds of Gehinnom rule over him" (Nedarim 22a). And they further said: "Whoever is angry – even the Shekhina is not important to him" (Nedarim 22b). And Eliyahu said to Rav Yehuda: do not become angry and you will not sin (Berakhot 29b).

But a person is permitted to show himself angry in order to instil fear in the members of his household so that they behave properly. As Rav Yehuda made himself very angry and tore his garment when the members of his household behaved improperly. Admittedly, he tore a garment that was already damaged anyway, or he only pulled a thread from it, in a way that it would afterwards be easy to repair. And Rav Aḥa bar Yaakov would break vessels to show how much their deeds angered him, and in truth these were broken vessels (Shabbat 105b).

The question is whether a person is forbidden to feel very bad about a negative act done against him or about an act of injustice, to the point that he feels his blood rising to his head. Seemingly from the words of the Rambam it is implied that it is forbidden. And so he wrote in Laws of Character Traits (2:3): "And there are traits in which a person is forbidden to conduct himself in the middle way; rather, he should distance himself from one extreme to the other extreme, and that is haughtiness etc. And likewise anger is an exceedingly bad trait, and it is fitting for a person to distance himself from it to the other extreme, and to teach himself not to become angry, even over something about which it is fitting to be angry. And if he wishes to instil fear in his children and the members of his household, or in the public if he is a leader, and wishes to be angry with them so that they return to the good, he should show himself before them as being angry in order to discipline them, while his mind is settled within himself, like a person who imitates an angry man at the time of his anger while he is not angry. The early Sages said: whoever is angry is as if he worships the stars; and they said that whoever is angry – if he is a sage, his wisdom departs from him, and if he is a prophet, his prophecy departs from him; and the life of angry people is no life. Therefore they commanded to distance oneself from anger until one accustoms oneself not to feel even things that cause anger, and this is the good way, etc."

And seemingly it is difficult: how does the Torah want a person to care about the repair of the world, and yet when acts of injustice are done before him, he should not seethe? And likewise we find that after Moshe Rabbeinu saw the calf and the dancing, his anger burned and he broke the tablets (Shemot 32:19). And likewise it is said of Shaul, when he heard of the evil deeds of Naḥash the Ammonite: "And the spirit of God came mightily upon Shaul when he heard those words, and his anger was kindled greatly" (I Shmuel 11:6), and he went out to fight the Ammonites and brought salvation to Israel. And likewise we find in the Torah several times burning anger on the part of Hashem. And this is not the place to detail all the places in which burning anger is mentioned in a positive way. Admittedly, it cannot be denied that many times the burning anger and wrath that appear in Tanakh express a certain loss of control and bad deeds (see also the wrath of Moshe at the sons of Aharon in Vayikra 10:16, and at the officers of the army in Bamidbar 31:14).

And indeed it is said in the Zohar (part 1, 184a, in translation): "There is anger and there is anger: there is anger that is blessed above and below, and there is anger that is cursed above and below."

Personal emotional involvement is a positive thing, and when anger causes positive, corrective action, it has value. But when anger causes a person to lose his judgement, to the point that he may do things he will afterwards greatly regret, then his soul has fallen captive to anger. And this is an aspect of idolatry, that at that time only one thing interests and occupies him, like idolaters who serve one of the forces of nature. The test for this: when a person is angry about something that a certain person did, how will he react if in the midst of his anger they say to him, but that person also did good deeds? If he admits the truth and says, even so, about this particular thing I am angry, then he is sane; but if he denies every good thing that he did, this is the angry man who is like an idolater.

And this is the example that the Sages gave: that a person begins to break his vessels from the greatness of his anger, so that instead of doing something useful he begins to harm himself. And such behaviour is permitted only if it is done outwardly only. But when a person speaks with warmth and emotion about things that stir his heart, and is prepared to exert himself greatly to repair them, there is no flaw in this, and this is the positive fervour.

It follows that according to the Rambam, because of the danger of the trait of anger, it is right to go against it to the furthest extreme; and one must distance oneself from all anger, even when it is under control and rouses to repair. But from the plain meaning of the verses and the words of the Sages, and likewise according to the words of the Zohar, it follows that a person is not obligated to try not to be angry at bad deeds; rather, he is obligated to control his anger, and not to let anger lead him to deeds that are not sane.[2]

notes_en.en: Our master Rabbi Kook wrote in Ein Aya, Berakhot ch. 1, 69: "They taught us that among all the traits that Hashem engraved in the nature of man and his soul, there is not one that is absolutely bad, such that it would be good for the soul to be without it. For the good Maker made everything for good. One need only use each one at its time and in its measure. From this it follows that one should not suppress even the bad trait too much, in such a way as not to give it any place; rather, it is fitting to give it its limited place and to try to correct it. Therefore one does not appease a person at the time of his anger, for the complete person too may become angry. Therefore the trait of anger must exist, and it is fitting to be appeased immediately; but to say that anger should have no place at all implies as if a power had been created in the soul for evil, and this cannot be said (and the words of the Ḥasid in Mesillat Yesharim ch. 11, who wrote that the virtue of the pure and excellent person is that anger should never make any impression on him at all, require examination in my humble opinion)."
